solution:
The field at the centre of a tightly wound circular coil of \(N\) turns is
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 N I}{2R}\)
Here \(N = 100\), \(I = 0.40\,\text{A}\) and \(R = 8.0\,\text{cm} = 8.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\).
\(B = \dfrac{4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 100 \times 0.40}{2 \times 8.0 \times 10^{-2}}\)
\(B = 3.1 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{T}\)
Its direction is along the axis of the coil, given by the right-hand thumb rule.

Answer: \(B = 3.1 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{T}\) at the centre, directed along the axis of the coil.

For a long straight wire, Ampere's circuital law gives
\(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\)
Here \(I = 35\,\text{A}\) and \(r = 20\,\text{cm} = 0.20\,\text{m}\), and \(\mu_0/2\pi = 2 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{T m A}^{-1}\).
\(B = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 35}{0.20} = 3.5 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{T}\)
The field lines are circles concentric with the wire, so \(\mathbf{B}\) is tangential to the circle of radius \(20\,\text{cm}\) through the point.

Answer: \(B = 3.5 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{T}\).

Magnitude, from \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\) with \(I = 50\,\text{A}\) and \(r = 2.5\,\text{m}\):
\(B = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 50}{2.5} = 4 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{T}\)
Direction, by the right-hand rule: grasp the wire with the right thumb pointing along the current, i.e. towards the south. The fingers then curl so that on the eastern side of the wire they point upwards. Taking east as \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\), north as \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\) and vertically up as \(\hat{\mathbf{z}}\), the current is along \(-\hat{\mathbf{y}}\) and the point lies along \(+\hat{\mathbf{x}}\), so \(\mathbf{B} \propto (-\hat{\mathbf{y}}) \times \hat{\mathbf{x}} = +\hat{\mathbf{z}}\).

Answer: \(B = 4 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{T}\), directed vertically upwards.

Magnitude, from \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}\) with \(I = 90\,\text{A}\) and \(r = 1.5\,\text{m}\):
\(B = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 90}{1.5} = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{T}\)
Direction: take east as \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}\), north as \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}\) and up as \(\hat{\mathbf{z}}\). The current flows east to west, i.e. along \(-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\), and the point lies below the line, along \(-\hat{\mathbf{z}}\). Then \(\mathbf{B} \propto (-\hat{\mathbf{x}}) \times (-\hat{\mathbf{z}}) = \hat{\mathbf{x}} \times \hat{\mathbf{z}} = -\hat{\mathbf{y}}\), which points south.

Answer: \(B = 1.2 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{T}\), directed towards the south.

The force on a straight current-carrying wire in a uniform field is \(\mathbf{F} = I\boldsymbol{l} \times \mathbf{B}\), so the force per unit length is
\(f = \dfrac{F}{l} = I B \sin\theta\)
With \(I = 8\,\text{A}\), \(B = 0.15\,\text{T}\) and \(\theta = 30^{\circ}\),
\(f = 8 \times 0.15 \times \sin 30^{\circ} = 8 \times 0.15 \times 0.5\)
\(f = 0.6\,\text{N m}^{-1}\)
The force is perpendicular to both the wire and the field.

Answer: \(f = 0.6\,\text{N m}^{-1}\).

Inside the solenoid the field is uniform and along the axis, and the wire is perpendicular to that axis, so \(\theta = 90^{\circ}\) and
\(F = I l B \sin\theta = I l B\)
With \(I = 10\,\text{A}\), \(l = 3.0\,\text{cm} = 3.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\) and \(B = 0.27\,\text{T}\),
\(F = 10 \times 3.0 \times 10^{-2} \times 0.27 = 8.1 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N}\)
By \(\mathbf{F} = I\boldsymbol{l} \times \mathbf{B}\) the force is perpendicular to both the wire and the solenoid axis.

Answer: \(F = 8.1 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{N}\), perpendicular to both the wire and the axis of the solenoid.

Wire B sets up a field at the location of wire A of magnitude \(B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_B}{2\pi d}\), so the force per unit length on A is
\(\dfrac{F}{l} = \dfrac{\mu_0 I_A I_B}{2\pi d}\)
With \(I_A = 8.0\,\text{A}\), \(I_B = 5.0\,\text{A}\) and \(d = 4.0\,\text{cm} = 4.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\),
\(\dfrac{F}{l} = \dfrac{2 \times 10^{-7} \times 8.0 \times 5.0}{4.0 \times 10^{-2}} = 2 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{N m}^{-1}\)
For a section of length \(l = 10\,\text{cm} = 0.10\,\text{m}\),
\(F = 2 \times 10^{-4} \times 0.10 = 2 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{N}\)
The currents are in the same direction, so the force is attractive, i.e. directed towards wire B.

Answer: \(F = 2 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{N}\), attractive (directed towards wire B).

The solenoid has \(5\) layers of \(400\) turns each, so the total number of turns is \(5 \times 400 = 2000\) over a length \(l = 80\,\text{cm} = 0.80\,\text{m}\). The number of turns per unit length is
\(n = \dfrac{2000}{0.80} = 2500\ \text{turns m}^{-1}\)
The diameter \(1.8\,\text{cm}\) is very much smaller than the length \(80\,\text{cm}\), so the long-solenoid result applies near the centre:
\(B = \mu_0 n I = 4\pi \times 10^{-7} \times 2500 \times 8.0\)
\(B = 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{T}\)
The field is directed along the axis of the solenoid.

Answer: \(B = 2.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{T}\) near the centre, along the axis.

The magnetic moment of the coil is \(m = N I A\) and the torque in a uniform field is \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{m} \times \mathbf{B}\), so
\(\tau = N I A B \sin\theta\)
where \(\theta\) is the angle between the normal to the coil and \(\mathbf{B}\), which is given as \(30^{\circ}\).
Area \(A = (10\,\text{cm})^{2} = (0.10\,\text{m})^{2} = 1.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}^{2}\).
\(\tau = 20 \times 12 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-2} \times 0.80 \times \sin 30^{\circ}\)
\(\tau = 20 \times 12 \times 1.0 \times 10^{-2} \times 0.80 \times 0.5 = 0.96\,\text{N m}\)

Answer: \(\tau = 0.96\,\text{N m}\).

For a moving coil meter with torsion constant \(k\), the equilibrium deflection satisfies \(k\phi = N I A B\).
Current sensitivity \(= \dfrac{\phi}{I} = \dfrac{N A B}{k}\), and voltage sensitivity \(= \dfrac{\phi}{V} = \dfrac{N A B}{k R}\).
The spring constants are identical, so \(k\) cancels in every ratio.

(a) Ratio of current sensitivities:
\(\dfrac{(\phi/I)_2}{(\phi/I)_1} = \dfrac{N_2 A_2 B_2}{N_1 A_1 B_1} = \dfrac{42 \times 1.8 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.50}{30 \times 3.6 \times 10^{-3} \times 0.25} = \dfrac{3.78 \times 10^{-2}}{2.70 \times 10^{-2}} = 1.4\)

(b) Ratio of voltage sensitivities:
\(\dfrac{(\phi/V)_2}{(\phi/V)_1} = \dfrac{N_2 A_2 B_2}{N_1 A_1 B_1} \times \dfrac{R_1}{R_2} = 1.4 \times \dfrac{10}{14} = 1.0\)

Answer: (a) current sensitivity of \(M_2\) is \(1.4\) times that of \(M_1\); (b) the voltage sensitivities are equal, ratio \(= 1.0\).

[Textbook misprint in the QUESTION, and this one is answer-affecting: the stem gives the electron's charge as \(e = 1.5 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\). The elementary charge is \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\), and the book's answer key is computed with that value — \(r = m_e v/(eB)\) gives \(4.2\,\text{cm}\) with \(1.6\), and \(4.48\,\text{cm}\) with the printed \(1.5\). THE CHAPTER CONTRADICTS ITSELF: its own Example 4.3 prints the electron charge as \(1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\). The stem is transcribed as printed; the solution below works it through and states both values so either can be followed.] The electron is shot normal to \(\mathbf{B}\), so the magnetic force \(\mathbf{F} = -e(\mathbf{v} \times \mathbf{B})\) is perpendicular to \(\mathbf{v}\) at every instant. A force that is always perpendicular to the velocity does no work, so the speed stays constant; it only turns the velocity, and being of constant magnitude \(evB\) it supplies a constant centripetal force. A constant-speed motion under a constant centripetal force is uniform circular motion, so the path is a circle in the plane normal to \(\mathbf{B}\).

Equating the magnetic force to the centripetal force,
\(evB = \dfrac{m_e v^{2}}{r}\), so \(r = \dfrac{m_e v}{eB}\)
Here \(B = 6.5\,\text{G} = 6.5 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{T}\), \(v = 4.8 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\) and \(m_e = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg}\).
Using the charge \(e = 1.5 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\) as printed in the question,
\(r = \dfrac{9.1 \times 10^{-31} \times 4.8 \times 10^{6}}{1.5 \times 10^{-19} \times 6.5 \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{4.37 \times 10^{-24}}{9.75 \times 10^{-23}} = 4.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\)

Answer: the path is a circle because the magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity, so it changes only the direction of motion and acts as a constant centripetal force. Radius \(r = 4.5 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m} = 4.5\,\text{cm}\) using the value \(e = 1.5 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\) printed in the question; with the true electronic charge \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\) the same calculation gives \(r = 4.2 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m} = 4.2\,\text{cm}\).
_note: The printed stem gives e = 1.5 x 10^-19 C, which is not the elementary charge (1.6 x 10^-19 C, the value this same chapter uses in Example 4.3). The discrepancy is answer-affecting (4.5 cm vs 4.2 cm), so the solution derives with the printed value and states both. Flagged for the answer-key cross-check; not silently corrected.

solution:
The electron of Exercise 4.11 moves in a circle of radius \(r = m_e v/(eB)\) with speed \(v\), so the period is
\(T = \dfrac{2\pi r}{v} = \dfrac{2\pi m_e}{eB}\)
and the frequency of revolution is
\(\nu = \dfrac{1}{T} = \dfrac{eB}{2\pi m_e}\)
The speed \(v\) has cancelled: a faster electron travels a proportionally larger circle, so it takes the same time to go round.

With \(B = 6.5 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{T}\), \(m_e = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg}\) and the charge \(e = 1.5 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\) printed in Exercise 4.11,
\(\nu = \dfrac{1.5 \times 10^{-19} \times 6.5 \times 10^{-4}}{2\pi \times 9.1 \times 10^{-31}} = \dfrac{9.75 \times 10^{-23}}{5.72 \times 10^{-30}} = 1.7 \times 10^{7}\,\text{Hz}\)

Answer: \(\nu = \dfrac{eB}{2\pi m_e} = 1.7 \times 10^{7}\,\text{Hz} = 17\,\text{MHz}\) using the charge \(e = 1.5 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\) printed in Exercise 4.11; with the true electronic charge \(e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}\) it is \(1.8 \times 10^{7}\,\text{Hz} = 18\,\text{MHz}\). No, the frequency does not depend on the speed of the electron — the speed cancels between the orbit's circumference and the time taken to cover it, which is why this cyclotron frequency is the same for all speeds (in the non-relativistic regime).
_note: Inherits the e = 1.5 x 10^-19 C misprint from Exercise 4.11, which this stem refers to for its data. Both values are stated; the printed-data result is 17 MHz and the standard-charge result is 18 MHz.

solution:
The coil has magnetic moment \(m = N I A\), and in a uniform field the torque on it is \(\boldsymbol{\tau} = \mathbf{m} \times \mathbf{B}\). To hold the coil still, the applied counter torque must equal this magnetic torque in magnitude:
\(\tau = N I A B \sin\theta\)
where \(\theta\) is the angle between the normal to the coil and \(\mathbf{B}\), given as \(60^{\circ}\).
Area \(A = \pi r^{2} = \pi (8.0 \times 10^{-2})^{2} = 2.01 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}^{2}\).
\(m = N I A = 30 \times 6.0 \times 2.01 \times 10^{-2} = 3.62\,\text{A m}^{2}\)
\(\tau = 3.62 \times 1.0 \times \sin 60^{\circ} = 3.62 \times 0.866\)
\(\tau = 3.1\,\text{N m}\)

Answer: the counter torque required is \(\tau = 3.1\,\text{N m}\).

No, the answer would not change.
The torque depends on the coil only through its magnetic moment \(m = N I A\), and for any PLANAR loop the area vector has magnitude equal to the enclosed area \(A\) and direction along the normal to its plane — the shape of the boundary does not enter. This can be seen by dividing the irregular loop into a mesh of small rectangles carrying the same current \(I\): the currents in every shared internal edge are equal and opposite and cancel, leaving only the current in the outer boundary, so the loop is equivalent to the sum of those elementary loops and its moment is \(I\) times the total enclosed area.
Since \(N\), \(I\), \(A\), \(B\) and the angle \(\theta = 60^{\circ}\) are all unaltered, \(\tau = N I A B \sin\theta\) is unchanged.

Answer: No — the counter torque is unchanged at \(3.1\,\text{N m}\), because the torque depends only on the enclosed area (through \(m = N I A\)) and not on the shape of a planar coil.
